title: The Virtual Destructor Rule
key_points: `delete p` calls the destructor of the *static* type (`Base`) unless the destructor is virtual.
So `~Derived` never runs, and `Derived`'s members (here the vector's heap buffer) are never released.
Formally, deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour, not just a leak.
Rule: if a class is meant to be deleted polymorphically (it has virtual functions / is a base class), give it a public virtual destructor. Otherwise make the destructor protected and non-virtual.
model_answer:
Without `virtual`, `delete p` is bound at compile time to `Base::~Base`, because `p` has static type `Base*`. `Derived::~Derived` never runs, so the `std::vector` member is never destroyed and its heap buffer leaks. More precisely, the standard says this is **undefined behaviour**: the leak is just the most common symptom.

Making `~Base` virtual puts the destructor in the vtable. `delete p` then dispatches to `~Derived`, which runs and then automatically calls `~Base`, the correct reverse order.

The guideline (Herb Sutter, C++ Core Guidelines C.35): a base class destructor should be either **public and virtual** (if you'll delete through a base pointer) or **protected and non-virtual** (if you won't, which stops anyone trying). Since `Base` already has a virtual function, it already has a vptr, so making the destructor virtual costs essentially nothing.
